topicName: Basic Git Commands: init, clone, add, commit, status, diff
content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Basic Git Commands: init, clone, add, commit, status, diff"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"This tutorial covers the fundamental Git commands necessary for version control: `init`, `clone`, `add`, `commit`, `status`, and `diff`. These commands form the basis for managing changes in your projects."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. git init: Initializing a Repository"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `git init` command creates a new Git repository. It's the first step in version-controlling an existing project or starting a new one."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"git init"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command creates a hidden `.git` folder in your project's root directory. This folder contains all the necessary repository metadata."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"2. git clone: Cloning a Repository"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `git clone` command creates a local copy of a remote repository. This is how you obtain a project from platforms like GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"git clone <repository_url>"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Replace `<repository_url>` with the URL of the remote repository you want to clone. For example: `git clone https://github.com/user/repository.git`"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"3. git add: Staging Changes"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `git add` command stages changes for the next commit. Staging means telling Git which changes you want to include in your next snapshot."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"git add <file>\ngit add ."},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"`git add <file>` stages a specific file. `git add .` stages all modified and new files in the current directory and its subdirectories."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"4. git commit: Committing Changes"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `git commit` command saves the staged changes to the repository with a descriptive message. A commit represents a snapshot of your project at a specific point in time."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"git commit -m \"Your commit message here\""},{"order":18,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `-m` flag allows you to include a commit message directly in the command.  Write clear and concise commit messages to explain the changes you've made. For example: `git commit -m \"Fix: Resolved issue with user authentication\"`"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"5. git status: Checking Repository Status"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `git status` command displays the state of the working directory and the staging area. It shows which files have been modified, staged, or are untracked."},{"order":21,"type":"code","text":"git status"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"This command is essential for understanding the current state of your repository and ensuring you're committing the correct changes."},{"order":23,"type":"subheading","text":"6. git diff: Viewing Changes"},{"order":24,"type":"paragraph","text":"The `git diff` command shows the differences between files in the working directory, staging area, and previous commits. It helps you review your changes before committing."},{"order":25,"type":"code","text":"git diff\ngit diff --staged"},{"order":26,"type":"paragraph","text":"`git diff` shows the changes in your working directory that are not yet staged. `git diff --staged` shows the changes that are staged but not yet committed."},{"order":27,"type":"paragraph","text":"These basic commands are the foundation for using Git effectively. Mastering them will allow you to manage your code, collaborate with others, and track changes efficiently."}]
